q: Which data type is most appropriate for storing the number of pupils in a class?
ms: C — pupils are COUNTED in whole numbers, so integer. Rule: count → int, measure → float, text → string, yes/no → Boolean.

q: Which data type is most appropriate for storing the price £4.99?
ms: B — money needs a decimal point, and only real/float can hold 4.99. An integer would lose the .99.

q: Which data type is most appropriate for storing a UK phone number such as 07700 900123?
ms: C — the leading 0 would be dropped by a numeric type, it contains a space, and you never do arithmetic on it. If you wouldn't add it, don't store it as a number.

q: Which data type holds only the values True and False?
ms: A — Boolean is the two-state type, perfect for flags like found or game_over.

q: In Python, the value `7.0` is of type
ms: B — the decimal point makes it a float even though the value looks whole. The point decides, not the value.

q: `marks = [56, 72, 39, 88]`. The value of `marks[1]` is
ms: B — indexing starts at 0, so index 1 is the SECOND item, 72. The index is the number of steps from the start.

q: `marks = [56, 72, 39, 88]`. The value of `len(marks)` is
ms: B — len counts the items: 4. But remember the last INDEX is 3 (len − 1).

q: `marks = [56, 72, 39, 88]`. Which line causes a runtime error?
ms: C — valid indexes run 0 to 3 (len − 1). marks[4] is one past the end: IndexError, a runtime error.

q: Which statement adds the value 65 to the end of the list `marks`?
ms: B — append is the list method that grows the list by one item at the end.

q: `grid = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]`. The value of `grid[1][2]` is
ms: C — RC: Row first, Column second. Row 1 is [4, 5, 6]; column 2 of that row is 6.

q: `grid = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]`. The value of `grid[0][1]` is
ms: B — row 0 is [1, 2, 3]; its index 1 is 2. Compare grid[1][0] = 4 — order matters!

q: A value that must not change while the program runs should be stored as a
ms: B — a constant, written in CAPITALS by convention (e.g. VAT_RATE = 0.2), signals 'do not change me'.

q: `word = "python"`. The value of `word[0]` is
ms: A — strings index like lists from 0, so word[0] is the first character, "p".

q: `word = "python"`. The value of `word[2:4]` is
ms: A — a slice runs from the start index UP TO BUT NOT INCLUDING the stop: positions 2 and 3 = "th".

q: Which is the best data structure for a 6-row × 8-seat cinema seating plan?
ms: C — a table of rows and columns maps naturally onto a 2D list: plan[row][seat].

q: Which is the best structure for the 20 test marks of one class?
ms: B — many values of the SAME type under one name; a loop can then process them all. 20 variables would need 20 lines of near-identical code.

q: A record for one product holds (name, price, in_stock). The types are
ms: A — name is text, price needs decimals, in_stock is a yes/no flag. Records mix types because each field means something different.

q: `nums = [4, 8, 15]`. After `nums[0] = 9`, the list is
ms: A — assigning to an index REPLACES that item. Lists are mutable (changeable), unlike strings.

q: `word = "cat"`. The line `word[0] = "h"` causes
options: a runtime error, because strings are immutable
ms: C — strings cannot be changed in place (immutable); the line runs and crashes with a TypeError. To 'change' a string you build a new one: word = "h" + word[1:].

q: `len("hello world")` returns
ms: B — len counts EVERY character including the space: 11. Spaces count!

q: The last valid index of a list `data` is always
ms: B — indexing starts at 0, so a 5-item list has indexes 0–4. len is a count; the top index is one less.

q: Which loop visits every item of `prices` regardless of its length?
ms: A — for-each iterates the actual items and automatically adapts to ANY list length — a key advantage of lists.

q: `temps = [12.5, 14.0, 9.8]`. The items are of type
ms: C — each value has a decimal point, so real/float — right for measured temperatures.

options: a string and an integer respectively
ms: B — quotes make "42" text. "42" + "1" gives "421" but 42 + 1 gives 43 — the type changes what + means.

q: In `grid[r][c]`, the first index selects the
ms: B — RC: Row then Column. The first bracket picks which inner list (row); the second picks the position inside it.

q: `word = "EXAM"`. `word.lower()` returns
ms: A — lower() returns a NEW all-lowercase string (the original is unchanged — strings are immutable).

q: Which is a sensible constant?
ms: B — the maximum number of lives is fixed for the whole game; CAPITALS signal it shouldn't change. The others all vary while running.
B — index 1 holds the whole inner list [4, 5]. To reach the 5 you'd write data[1][1].

q: A weather app stores whether it rained each day of a 7-day week. The best structure is
ms: B — one yes/no per day = a list of 7 Booleans, e.g. rained[3] for Thursday.

q: `scores = [10, 20, 30]`. `scores[len(scores) - 1]` is
ms: C — len − 1 is the standard way to reach the LAST item safely: index 2 → 30.

q: Which expression counts the characters in the string variable `name`?
ms: C — len() is a function you wrap AROUND the value: len(name).

q: A 2D list `board` has 4 rows and 5 columns. `len(board)` and `len(board[0])` are
ms: B — len(board) counts rows (4); len(board[0]) counts the items in the first row, i.e. columns (5).

q: Which value should be stored as a Boolean?
ms: B — 'was it correct?' has exactly two states, True/False. The password itself is a string; the counts are integers.

q: State the most appropriate data type for a person's height in metres (e.g. 1.75), and justify your choice. (2)
ms: Real/float (1) because height is a MEASURED value needing decimal places — an integer would lose the .75 (1). Pattern: count → int, measure → float.

q: State the most appropriate data type for a car registration such as "BD51 SMR", and justify your choice. (2)
ms: String (1) because it mixes letters, digits and a space, and no arithmetic is ever done on it (1). Like phone numbers: looks like it has numbers, but it's text.

q: Explain the difference between a variable and a constant, giving one example of each from a shopping program. (2)
ms: A variable's value can change during the run — e.g. basket_total goes up with each item (1); a constant's value is fixed for the whole run — e.g. VAT_RATE = 0.2 (1). Both are named memory locations; only the 'allowed to change' rule differs.

q: Give two advantages of storing 30 test marks in a list rather than in 30 separate variables. (2)
ms: Any two: one loop can process every mark using a single name, instead of 30 near-identical lines (1); the code works for ANY number of marks — adding a pupil doesn't mean writing new code (1); related data is kept together under one meaningful name (1).

q:
`items = ["pen", "ruler", "rubber", "pencil"]`

State the value of `items[2]` and the index of "pen". (2)
ms: items[2] = "rubber" — count 0: pen, 1: ruler, 2: rubber (1); "pen" is at index 0 — the first item always is (1).

q: A list holds 12 values. State its first and last valid index, and the expression that always gives the last index for any list `L`. (2)
ms: First 0, last 11 (1); len(L) - 1 (1). len counts items; indexes start at 0, so the top index is one less than the count.

q: Explain why `print(nums[len(nums)])` always crashes, and name the error type. (2)
ms: len(nums) is one PAST the last valid index (which is len − 1), so the item doesn't exist (1); runtime error — IndexError (1). Classic off-by-one.

q:
`board = [["X", "O", "X"], ["O", "O", "X"], ["X", "X", "O"]]`

State the values of `board[0][2]`, `board[2][0]` and `board[1][1]`. (3)
ms: board[0][2] = "X" — row 0 is [X, O, X], its index 2 (1); board[2][0] = "X" — row 2 is [X, X, O], its index 0 (1); board[1][1] = "O" — the centre (1). RC: Row first, Column second — [0][2] and [2][0] are different squares.

q: A pupil record stores (surname, form group letter, attendance %). State an appropriate data type for each field. (2)
ms: surname: string; form group letter: character/string (1); attendance %: real/float — e.g. 96.5 needs a decimal (accept integer if justified as whole-number %) (1).

q:
`word = "keyboard"`

State the value of `word[3]` and of `len(word)`. (2)
ms: word[3] = "b" — k(0) e(1) y(2) b(3) (1); len = 8 characters (1). len is a count, index is a position.

q:
`word = "keyboard"`

State the value of `word[0:3]` and explain why it is not 4 characters long. (2)
ms: "key" (1); the slice stops BEFORE index 3 — start is included, stop is excluded, so positions 0, 1, 2 only (1).

q: Describe what a record is, and how it differs from a list of marks. (2)
ms: A record groups several fields of DIFFERENT types that describe one entity, e.g. ("Ada", 15, 87.5) for one pupil (1); a list of marks holds many values of the SAME type, one per pupil (1).

q: Give one reason `True` is a different value from the string `"True"` in Python, and one error that confusing them could cause. (2)
ms: True is a Boolean (two-state type); "True" is text — quotes make the difference (1); e.g. if flag == "True": never matches a real Boolean flag, so the branch silently never runs — a logic error (1).

q:
A program stores daily rainfall (mm, decimals) for 4 weeks, one value per day.

State an appropriate data structure, its dimensions, and the expression for week 3 day 2's value (counting from 1). (3)
ms: A 2D list of floats (1); 4 rows × 7 columns — rain[week][day] (1); with 0-based indexing, week 3 day 2 is rain[2][1] (1). Subtract 1 from human counting to get the index.

q: State what `nums.append(7)` does to `nums = [1, 2]`, and give the resulting list and new length. (2)
ms: Adds 7 to the END of the list (1); result [1, 2, 7], length 3 (1).

q: Explain why `total = "12" + 5` fails but `total = int("12") + 5` works, naming the concepts involved. (2)
ms: "12" is a string, and + cannot join a string to an integer — a type mismatch (runtime TypeError) (1); int("12") CONVERTS (casts) the text to the integer 12 so numeric addition gives 17 (1).

q:
A quiz program uses `QUESTIONS = 10` at the top, then `range(QUESTIONS)` and `score / QUESTIONS` later.

Explain two benefits of this constant, and what a programmer must do to make the quiz 20 questions long. (3)
ms: The name explains what 10 means, making code readable (1); the value lives in ONE place, so every use stays consistent (1); change just the one line to QUESTIONS = 20 and the loop and the average both update automatically (1).

q:
Complete the sentence.

Whole numbers such as -3, 0 and 42 are stored using the ______ data type. (1)
ms: integer (1). Count → int.

q:
Complete the sentence.

Numbers with a decimal part, such as 9.81, are stored using the ______ data type. (1)
ms: real / float (1). Measure → float.

q:
Complete the sentence.

Text such as "Hello" is stored using the ______ data type. (1)
ms: string (1).

q:
Complete the sentence.

List indexing starts at position ______, so the last item of an n-item list is at index ______. (1)
ms: 0 and n − 1 (1). len is a count; the top index is one less.

q:
Complete the sentences.

A value that changes while the program runs is stored in a ______. A named value that stays fixed for the whole run is a ______. (2)
ms: variable (1); constant (1).

q:
Match each item of data to its best type.

**1** "Is the door locked?"  **2** A postcode  **3** A golf score of -2

**A** integer  **B** Boolean  **C** string (3)
ms: 1 → B: two states only (1); 2 → C: letters + digits, no arithmetic (1); 3 → A: a whole number that can be negative (1).

q:
Match each need to the best structure.

**1** 25 quiz scores, all integers  **2** One product's (name, price, stock flag)  **3** A chessboard's 8 × 8 squares

**A** record  **B** 2D list  **C** 1D list (3)
ms: 1 → C: many same-type values (1); 2 → A: mixed fields about one entity (1); 3 → B: a table needs row AND column (1).

q:
Match each expression to its value for `word = "computer"`.

**1** word[0]  **2** word[3:6]  **3** len(word)

**A** 8  **B** "c"  **C** "put" (3)
ms: 1 → B: index 0 is the first character (1); 2 → C: positions 3, 4, 5 — the stop is excluded (1); 3 → A: 8 characters counted (1).

q:
`prices = [2.50, 3.99, 1.20]`

State the output of:

`print(prices[1] + prices[2])` (2)
ms: 5.19 (2) — index 1 is 3.99 (the SECOND item), index 2 is 1.20; 3.99 + 1.20. Award 1 for adding 2.50 + 3.99 = 6.49 (forgot zero-indexing) with working.

q:
State the output.

`names = ["Amy", "Ben", "Cal"]`
`names[1] = "Bea"`
`print(names)` (2)
ms: ['Amy', 'Bea', 'Cal'] (2) — assigning to index 1 REPLACES "Ben"; lists are mutable. 1 mark if replacement at wrong position but concept shown.

q:
State the output.

`nums = [5, 10]`
`nums.append(15)`
`print(len(nums), nums[2])` (2)
ms: 3 15 (2) — append adds 15 at the end, making the length 3 and putting 15 at the new last index 2. 1 mark each part.

q:
State the output.

`total = 0`
`for n in [4, 7, 9]:`
`    total = total + n`
`print(total)` (2)
ms: 20 (2) — the for-each loop visits 4, 7, 9 in turn, accumulating 4 → 11 → 20. This one-loop pattern is WHY lists beat separate variables.

q:
State the output.

`word = "data"`
`print(word.upper())`
`print(word)` (2)
ms: DATA (1); then data — upper() returns a NEW string and the original is unchanged, because strings are immutable (1).

q:
`grid = [[2, 4], [6, 8], [10, 12]]`

State the values of `len(grid)`, `len(grid[0])` and `grid[2][1]`. (3)
ms: len(grid) = 3 — it counts ROWS (inner lists) (1); len(grid[0]) = 2 — items in the first row = columns (1); grid[2][1] = 12 — row 2 is [10, 12], its index 1 (1).

q:
A program needs yesterday's temperature to one decimal place and the number of hours of sunshine (whole hours).

State the best data type for each and the general rule you used. (2)
ms: Temperature: real/float; sunshine hours: integer (1); rule: measured values with decimals → float, counted whole values → int (1).

q: Explain why `if answer == True:` and `if answer == "yes":` test different kinds of variable, naming the type each expects. (2)
ms: The first compares a Boolean — answer holds True/False (1); the second compares a string — answer holds text the user typed (1). Mixing them up makes a condition that can never be True.

q:
State the output.

`letters = "abcdef"`
`print(letters[1])`
`print(letters[len(letters) - 1])` (2)
ms: b — index 1 is the second character (1); f — len − 1 = 5 is the last index (1).

q: A student writes `scores[3]` expecting the 3rd score. State what they actually get and the index they should use. (2)
ms: They get the 4th score — indexes count from 0, so index 3 is the fourth item (1); the 3rd score is scores[2] (1). Human position − 1 = index.

q: Write Python to: create a list `days` holding "Sat" and "Sun", append "Mon", then print the whole list. (3)
ms: days = ["Sat", "Sun"] (1); days.append("Mon") (1); print(days) → ['Sat', 'Sun', 'Mon'] (1).

q:
State the output.

`row = [3, 6, 9]`
`row[0] = row[0] + row[2]`
`print(row)` (2)
ms: [12, 6, 9] (2) — row[0] becomes 3 + 9 = 12; the other items are untouched. 1 mark for 12 computed.

q: Explain why a list is described as giving values "one name, many boxes", and what distinguishes each box. (2)
ms: All the items share the single list name, stored together (1); each item is distinguished by its index — its numbered position from 0 (1).

q:
State the output, showing the trace.

`nums = [2, 5, 8, 11]`
`total = 0`
`for i in range(len(nums)):`
`    if nums[i] % 2 == 0:`
`        total = total + nums[i]`
`print(total)` (3)
ms: Visits indexes 0–3 (1); even values are 2 and 8 — 5 and 11 fail the % 2 test (1); total = 10 (1).

q: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of `for n in nums:` compared with `for i in range(len(nums)):`. (2)
ms: Advantage: simpler/clearer — no index bookkeeping, no off-by-one risk (1); disadvantage: you don't know the POSITION, so you can't easily change items or report where a value was found (1).

q: A till stores today's transactions. State whether each should be a variable or constant: (a) `running_total` (b) `MAX_REFUND = 100`. (2)
ms: (a) variable — it changes with every sale (1); (b) constant — a fixed business rule for the whole day/run (1).

q:
State the output, showing the trace.

`grid = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]`
`total = 0`
`for row in grid:`
`    for item in row:`
`        total = total + item`
`print(total)` (3)
ms: Outer loop takes row = [1, 2] then [3, 4] (1); inner loop adds every item: 1+2+3+4 (1); output 10 (1). Nested loops are THE pattern for whole-table processing.

q:
State the output.

`name = "Ada Lovelace"`
`print(name[0] + name[4])` (2)
ms: AL (2) — index 0 is "A"; index 4 is "L" (the space at index 3 counts!). 1 mark if space miscounted but method right.

q:
Explain what happens here and why, naming the error.

`items = ["a", "b"]`
`print(items[2])` (2)
ms: The program crashes at run time with an IndexError (1) because valid indexes are 0 and 1 — index 2 is one past the end (len is 2, top index is 1) (1).

q:
A theatre has 3 price bands stored as `PRICES = [12.50, 9.00, 5.50]` and a booking `band = 1`.

State the ticket price selected, why a list beats three if-statements here, and the type of the values. (3)
ms: PRICES[1] = 9.00 (1); the band number IS the index, so one lookup line replaces a whole if/elif chain — and adding a band means editing data, not logic (1); real/float values — money needs decimals (1).

q:
State the output.

`flags = [True, False, True]`
`count = 0`
`for f in flags:`
`    if f:`
`        count = count + 1`
`print(count)` (2)
ms: 2 (2) — 'if f:' passes for each True; two of the three flags are True. Booleans can be tested directly without '== True'.

q: Write one line that prints the LAST character of any string variable `s`, and explain why it works for every length. (2)
ms: print(s[len(s) - 1]) (1); len adapts to the actual string, and −1 converts the count to the top index (1). (Accept s[-1] with the explanation that negative indexes count from the end.)

q:
A register is stored as `reg = [["Amy", True], ["Ben", False]]` — name and present-flag per pupil.

State the value of `reg[1][0]`, what `reg[0][1]` tells you, and what kind of structure each inner list is acting as. (3)
ms: reg[1][0] = "Ben" (1); reg[0][1] = True — Amy is present (1); each inner list acts as a RECORD: mixed types (string + Boolean) describing one pupil (1).

q:
State the output.

`s = "noon"`
`print(s[0] == s[3])`
`print(s[1] == s[2])` (2)
ms: True (1); True (1) — n = n and o = o; comparing end-pairs like this is exactly how palindrome checks work.

q: Why must a program cast `input()` before doing `marks[i] + 10`, and which cast is right for whole-number marks? (2)
ms: input() always returns a string, and a string can't be added to a number (TypeError) (1); int() — marks are counted whole numbers (1).

q:
State the output, showing the trace.

`values = [7, 2, 9, 4]`
`biggest = values[0]`
`for v in values:`
`    if v > biggest:`
`        biggest = v`
`print(biggest)` (3)
ms: Start biggest = 7 (1); 2 no, 9 yes → biggest = 9, 4 no (1); output 9 (1). The find-max pattern: seed with the first item, challenge with each other item.

q: A student stores a bank card PIN "0482" as an integer and later prints it. State what prints and why a string was the right choice. (2)
ms: 482 prints — an integer cannot keep the leading zero (1); a PIN is never used in arithmetic and its leading zero matters, so it's text: string (1).

q: Write Python that builds an empty list `evens`, then uses a loop over `range(1, 11)` to append only the even numbers, then prints the list. (3)
ms: evens = [] (1); for i in range(1, 11): if i % 2 == 0: evens.append(i) (1); print(evens) → [2, 4, 6, 8, 10] (1).

q:
State the output.

`word = "stream"`
`print(word[2:len(word)])` (2)
ms: ream (2) — slice from index 2 to the end (the stop equals len, which is excluded, exactly reaching the last character). 1 mark for "eam"/"team" with slicing idea shown.

q: A game board is `board[8][8]`. State how many squares that is and the index of the bottom-right square. (2)
ms: 64 squares (8 × 8) (1); board[7][7] — both indexes run 0 to 7 (1).

q:
Explain, step by step, what this code does and its output.

`first = "Grace"`
`last = "Hopper"`
`initials = first[0] + last[0]`
`print(initials)` (3)
ms: first[0] takes "G" (1); last[0] takes "H", and + joins the two 1-character strings (1); output GH (1). Indexing + concatenation = the initials pattern.

q: State two differences between how a list and a string behave when you try to change one element. (2)
ms: A list is mutable — nums[0] = 5 succeeds and changes the item in place (1); a string is immutable — s[0] = "x" raises a runtime TypeError; you must build a new string instead (1).

q:
State the output, showing your working.

`t = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]`
`print(t[0][2] + t[1][0])`
`print(t[1][2] - t[0][0])` (3)
ms: t[0][2] = 3 and t[1][0] = 4 → 7 (1); t[1][2] = 6 and t[0][0] = 1 → 5 (1); outputs on two lines: 7 then 5 (1). Always: Row first, Column second.

q: A survey stores 200 replies, each "Y" or "N". Suggest a more memory-conscious type than string for each reply and why. (2)
ms: Boolean — True for Y, False for N (1); a two-state fact fits the two-state type, is smaller and can be tested directly in conditions (1).

q:
State the output.

`stock = ["tea", "coffee", "milk"]`
`for i in range(len(stock)):`
`    print(i, stock[i])` (3)
ms: 0 tea (1); 1 coffee (1); 2 milk (1) — range(len) pairs each index with its item; this is the pattern when you need positions AND values.

q: Why does `range(len(nums))` never cause an IndexError when used as `nums[i]`, even though `nums[len(nums)]` does? (2)
ms: range stops BEFORE its stop value, so i runs 0 … len−1 — exactly the valid indexes (1); nums[len(nums)] asks directly for the index one past the end (1). Two off-by-one rules cancelling out perfectly.

q:
State the output.

`a = [1, 2]`
`b = [3, 4]`
`c = a + b`
`print(c)` (2)
ms: [1, 2, 3, 4] (2) — + on lists JOINS them into a new longer list (concatenation), just as it joins strings. 1 mark for the joining idea with wrong order.

q:
A school currently stores each pupil's five test marks in separate variables (amy1, amy2, … ben1, ben2 …) and writes separate totalling code for every pupil.

Discuss how using data structures could improve this program, naming the structures you would use. (6)
ms: Level-marked. Points: one pupil's five marks → a 1D list, so a single loop totals ANY pupil; all pupils → a 2D list (rows = pupils, columns = tests) or list of records (name + marks); one nested loop then processes the whole school; adding a pupil or a test becomes a data change, not new code; fewer variables → fewer naming mistakes; positions/indexes give direct access (marks[pupil][test]); code is shorter, clearer, easier to maintain and test. 5–6: several developed improvements with correct structures and access examples; 3–4: right structures with some development; 1–2: basic statements.

q:
State the output.

`s = "a"`
`s = s + "b"`
`s = s + "c"`
`print(s, len(s))` (2)
ms: abc 3 (2) — each line builds a NEW string one letter longer (strings can't change in place, but the variable can be re-pointed). 1 mark per part.

q: A temperature log must record below-freezing values like -4 and half degrees like 2.5 in ONE list. State the type the list should hold and why integer alone fails. (2)
ms: Real/float (1) — floats hold negatives AND decimal halves; integers would lose the .5 (2.5 would have to become 2 or 3) (1).

q:
State the output.

`row = [10, 20, 30]`
`row.append(row[0])`
`print(row)` (2)
ms: [10, 20, 30, 10] (2) — row[0] is read (10) and that VALUE is appended to the end. 1 mark for append understood but wrong value.

q: Design the data for a lunch till: item names, matching prices, and whether each item is vegetarian. Name the structure(s), how the three facts about one item stay linked, and the expression for the price of item at position `i`. (3)
ms: Parallel 1D lists (names, prices, veg flags) OR one list of records [name, price, veg] (1); linkage: the SAME index i refers to the same item in every list (or the same record row) (1); prices[i] — or items[i][1] for the record version (1).
